text: The sunken island empire described by Plato in his dialogues Timaeus and Critias (about 360 BC). Plato says the story reached Athens through the lawgiver Solon, who heard it from Egyptian priests at Sais: a great power beyond the Pillars of Hercules that made war on ancient Athens and vanished in a single day and night. Most scholars read it as a philosophical fable. In Verne's day, though, theories that it had really existed were popular, and Aronnax's long list of believers and doubters is a roll call of ancient and modern authorities.

A vast continent beyond the ocean invented by the Greek historian Theopompus of Chios (4th century BC). Its two cities were Machimos ("Warlike") and Eusebes ("Pious"), which is where Aronnax's "Makhimos" and "Eusebes" come from. The tale was probably a satire of Plato's Atlantis, but Aronnax takes it as supporting evidence.

The ancient name for the two headlands on either side of the Strait of Gibraltar: the Rock of Gibraltar and Jebel Musa in Morocco. For the Greeks they marked the edge of the known world, so "beyond the Pillars" meant out in the open Atlantic.

term: Madeira, the Azores, the Canaries, the Cape Verde Islands
text: Volcanic island groups in the Atlantic off Portugal and northwest Africa. Atlantis enthusiasts claimed them as the drowned continent's surviving mountaintops. The Atlantic floor really is volcanic, as Aronnax says, but the reason was only understood in the 1960s. Along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge the seafloor is slowly pulling apart and new crust is forming, and the Azores sit right on that ridge.
quote: Madeira, the Azores, the Canaries, the Cape Verde Islands

term: Pompeii, Vesuvius and Torre del Greco
text: The Roman town of Pompeii was buried by an eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79. In the 1860s its excavation was front-page news, especially the plaster casts of victims made from 1863 onward. Torre del Greco is a town at the foot of Vesuvius that lava flows overran again and again, worst of all in 1794. To Verne's readers, "a whole Pompeii" meant an entire city preserved by catastrophe.
quote: a whole Pompeii buried under the waters

text: A long wooden staff with an iron point, used by climbers in the Alps. It was the forerunner of the ice axe and the trekking pole. Nemo hands Aronnax one because their night walk includes climbing a mountain.
quote: an alpenstock being placed in my hand

text: Prehistoric stone tombs made of upright stones roofed with a huge flat slab. They are especially common in Brittany and would have been familiar to any French reader as the oldest human buildings they knew.
quote: like the dolmens of prehistoric times

text: Triremes: oared warships of ancient Greece with three banks of rowers on each side and a bronze ram at the bow. They were the battleships of the Athenian navy, so Aronnax is picturing a port fit for the Atlanteans' war with Athens.

The translator's word for Verne's "poulpe", an old name for the octopus. Verne uses it loosely for large cephalopods in general, squid included. The English name captures the dread that sailors and fishermen felt toward these many-armed animals.

A headland on the easternmost bulge of Brazil, near Natal. Sailing ships bound from Europe for the Cape of Good Hope swung far west toward it to pick up favorable winds before turning southeast. That's why sails are on the horizon in mid-Atlantic.

Jean Sylvain Bailly (1736–1793), a French astronomer who wrote a book of letters about Atlantis in 1779, placing it in the far north (hence the editor's footnote). He became the first mayor of Paris during the Revolution and was guillotined in 1793.

The Nautilus runs on electricity from sodium batteries, as Nemo explained to Aronnax earlier in the voyage. Nemo extracts the sodium from seawater by heating it with coal. That explains the chain he recites (coal makes sodium, sodium feeds batteries, batteries make electricity) and why he needs a secret coal mine. Sodium really was produced with coal-fired furnaces in the 1860s.

Newcastle upon Tyne in northeast England was the most famous coal district in the world, which is why "carrying coals to Newcastle" means doing something pointless. Some of the region's mines really did run out under the North Sea, so Nemo's undersea mine has a real-world model.

Dracaena draco, a strange umbrella-shaped tree native to the Canary Islands and nearby Atlantic islands. Its red resin, called "dragon's blood", was sold as a dye and medicine. Together with the bees "so common to all the Canary Islands", it's Aronnax's clue to roughly where the volcano is.
quote: a sturdy clump of dragon trees

text: Conglomerate: rock made of rounded pebbles cemented together, like the fruit in a plum pudding. Here they're loose, which is why the climb is so treacherous. Tuff, trachyte and obsidian, also mentioned, are all rocks formed by volcanoes.

Basalt is dark volcanic rock. When a thick lava flow cools slowly, it can crack into regular six-sided pillars, as at the Giant's Causeway in Ireland or Fingal's Cave in Scotland. That's the "natural architecture" holding up the cavern's vault.

In Scott's novel The Antiquary (1816), Sir Arthur Wardour and his daughter Isabella are cut off by the incoming tide at the foot of sea cliffs and rescued at the last moment. It was one of the best-known scenes in 19th-century fiction.
Small fish that bury themselves in sand with only their venomous back spines showing. Stepping on one is agonizing, and swimmers on European beaches still get stung.
quote: weevers known in Aristotle’s day as sea dragons

text: The powerful warm current that flows out of the Gulf of Mexico, up the American coast and across the Atlantic toward Europe. It helps give northwest Europe its mild climate. Verne's description of its branches is a little muddled, but the basic idea is right: it's one side of a huge clockwise circulation of the North Atlantic.
quote: known by name as the Gulf Stream

text: A calm region of the North Atlantic east of Bermuda, ringed by currents and covered with floating mats of sargassum seaweed. It's the only sea with no coastline. The weed actually lives and grows at sea rather than being torn from distant beaches. In the 1920s scientists found that European and American eels travel here to spawn.

Columbus's ships reached the Sargasso weed in September 1492. His crews feared it meant hidden shallows, but they also took it as a sign that land was near. Aronnax's "three long weeks" exaggerates how much it slowed them.

Matthew Fontaine Maury (1806–1873), the U.S. Navy officer called "the Pathfinder of the Seas". He built wind and current charts from thousands of ships' logs, and his Physical Geography of the Sea (1855) is often called the first oceanography textbook. Verne relies on him constantly. Some of Maury's theories, such as his ideas about the Gulf Stream's source and the poles, have since been abandoned.
The southern tip of South America, on a Chilean island. Its gales, huge waves and icebergs made it the most feared passage in the age of sail. To "double" a cape means to sail around it.

Ocean depth was measured by lowering a weighted line. Currents carried the line sideways, so it kept paying out without touching bottom. That's how Denham (HMS Herald) and Parker (USS Congress) reported 14,000–15,000 meters in the 1850s, figures now known to be wrong. The deepest point in the South Atlantic is about 8,300 meters, and the deepest anywhere, in the Pacific's Mariana Trench, is about 11,000. The Nautilus's 16,000-meter dive goes deeper than any real ocean.

A unit of pressure: one atmosphere is the weight of air at sea level, about 1 kilogram on every square centimeter. Water adds roughly one more atmosphere every 10 meters down. For comparison, the bathyscaphe Trieste, at the bottom of the Mariana Trench in 1960, faced about 1,100 atmospheres.

In Verne's day many naturalists believed that the deep ocean, below a few hundred fathoms, was lifeless (the "azoic" theory). In 1860 HMS Bulldog, surveying a route for a telegraph cable, hauled up starfish clinging to its line from more than 2,000 fathoms. That was some of the first hard evidence against the theory. (A fathom is six feet, about 1.8 meters.)

In 1868 photography meant glass plates and long exposures. The first underwater photograph was taken in 1856 by William Thompson in shallow water off southern England. A crisp picture of the abyssal floor was pure science fiction. Real ones came only in the 20th century.
quote: taking a photograph of this underwater region

text: The orca, which really is the largest member of the dolphin family. That's why Aronnax can call it a dolphin. It hunts seals, porpoises and even large whales. The "Copenhagen professor" is the Danish zoologist Daniel Eschricht, who reported the remains of over a dozen porpoises and seals in one orca's stomach.

Baleen whales have no teeth. They strain small creatures from the water through plates of "whalebone" (baleen) hanging from the upper jaw, which was valued for corsets and umbrella ribs. Sperm whales are toothed hunters that dive deep for squid. Nemo's contrast between "harmless" baleen whales and "cruel" sperm whales reflects the attitudes of his time.

A waxy oil filling a huge chamber in the sperm whale's head. It made the finest candles and lubricants and was the main reason sperm whales were hunted. The name ("whale seed") comes from an old belief that it was the whale's sperm.

Right whales got their name from whalers: they were the "right" whale to hunt because they swim slowly, stay near coasts and float when killed. By the 1860s they had been hunted to near-extinction. The bowhead Ned knows from the Arctic is a close relative. Aronnax's species distinctions are partly confused by modern standards.
quote: the southern right whale is still unknown to you

text: The Bering Strait separates Alaska from Siberia. The Davis Strait lies between Greenland and Baffin Island. Whalers hunted bowheads in both. Ned's harpooned whale really is evidence of an Arctic route linking the two, the way Aronnax suggests.
quote: the Bering Strait and the Davis Strait

text: A Nantucket whaleship rammed and sunk in the Pacific in November 1820. It was attacked by a sperm whale, not the baleen whale Aronnax describes. The survivors spent three months in open boats, some resorting to cannibalism. The disaster inspired Herman Melville's Moby-Dick (1851).

In the Arabian Nights, on Sinbad's first voyage, his crew land on a little island, light a fire and discover that it's a sleeping whale, which dives. The same legend appears in the medieval voyage of Saint Brendan. Aronnax is teasing Ned that his whale story is straight out of a fairy tale.
quote: Like in the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor

text: Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon (1707–1788), author of the 36-volume Natural History, the most widely read science book of the 18th century. By 1868 many of its claims, like whales living a thousand years, were badly out of date, which is Aronnax's point.
A jaunty American song from the Revolutionary War. Whistling it with his hands in his pockets is Ned's way of showing he's unimpressed by Nemo's lecture.

The Basques of northern Spain and southwest France were Europe's first commercial whalers. They hunted right whales in the Bay of Biscay from around the 11th century and crossed to Labrador by the 1500s, long before the English and Dutch joined in.
quote: first dragged the Basques in its wake

text: Whalers' slang for a herd (a "pod") of whales. It also meant a social visit between two whaling ships meeting at sea. Ned is using his old trade's vocabulary.

The translator's term for Verne's "banquise": the wall of pack ice, fused icebergs and ice shelves that surrounds Antarctica. In 1841 James Clark Ross met the Great Ice Barrier (now the Ross Ice Shelf), ice cliffs up to about 60 meters high. Sailing ships of Verne's day could push no farther, which is why Ned treats it as nature's final boundary.
A white glare on the underside of clouds, reflected from ice beyond the horizon. Polar sailors read it as a warning of pack ice ahead. The opposite, a dark "water sky", signaled open water.

term: icebergs, ice fields, drift ice, packs
text: The polar sailors' working vocabulary. Icebergs are floating mountains broken off glaciers. Ice fields are vast flat sheets of frozen sea. Drift ice is loose floating floes. Packs are jumbled broken ice crammed together. Conseil, the born classifier, is naturally delighted.

The line of latitude at about 66°33′ south. South of it the sun stays up for at least one full day at midsummer and stays down for at least one full day at midwinter. Only a handful of expeditions had crossed it by 1868.

term: South Shetland and South Orkney Islands
text: Bleak island groups off the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, discovered around 1819–1821. British and American sealers stripped them of their fur seals within a few seasons, so Nemo's bitter account is historically accurate.
quote: South Shetland and South Orkney Islands

text: A compass points to the magnetic poles, which are not at the geographic poles and slowly wander. Near a magnetic pole the needle tries to point down into the earth and becomes useless for steering. Hansteen and Duperrey were scientists who estimated its position. A party from Shackleton's expedition first reached it in 1909.

Fresh water is densest at about 4 °C, so the coldest water rises and lakes freeze from the top down. Aronnax assumes seawater behaves the same way, but ocean water actually keeps getting denser right down to its freezing point. His conclusion still holds: the ice floats and the water beneath it stays liquid.

Nemo's three feet below for every foot above is too low. Because ice is about 90 percent as dense as seawater, roughly seven to nine times as much of an iceberg lies below the surface as above it. That's where "the tip of the iceberg" comes from.
quote: For each foot of iceberg above the sea

text: Many 19th-century geographers, Maury among them, believed in an "open polar sea": ice-free water at the poles, kept warm by ocean currents beyond a ring of ice. Arctic expeditions were launched to find it. It doesn't exist. The Arctic is a frozen ocean, and Antarctica is a continent buried under ice up to four kilometers thick.
quote: why wouldn’t we find open sea at the South Pole

text: In 1868 no one had come within about 1,300 kilometers of the South Pole. It was first reached overland by Roald Amundsen's Norwegian party on December 14, 1911, five weeks ahead of Robert Falcon Scott. The real pole sits on an ice plateau about 2,800 meters high, hundreds of kilometers from any coast, with no open sea, volcanic shore, seals or penguins. Verne's polar landscape is educated guesswork.

term: Sir James Clark Ross, Erebus and Terror
text: A British naval officer whose 1839–1843 expedition in HMS Erebus and HMS Terror discovered Victoria Land, the Ross Sea and the great ice barrier, and named the active volcano Mount Erebus. His farthest south, 78°10′, stood for nearly 60 years. The same two ships were later lost with all hands in Franklin's Arctic expedition.

term: Nemo's roll call of Antarctic explorers
text: Nemo's list is broadly accurate to Verne's sources. Captain Cook first crossed the Antarctic Circle in 1773 but never saw the continent. Bellingshausen, a Russian, sighted its ice coast in 1820. James Weddell, a sealer, pushed into the sea now named for him. The Frenchman Dumont d'Urville named the Adélie Coast after his wife, and the Adélie penguin is named for it too.

At the pole the year is one long day and one long night. The sun circles the sky without setting from the September equinox to the March equinox, then disappears for six months. On March 21 it skims along the horizon all day, so seeing its disk cut exactly in half at noon, timed by a chronometer (a precision ship's clock), tells Nemo he's at the pole. Refraction is the bending of light by the air, which makes the sun look a little higher than it really is.
quote: Tomorrow, the 21st, was the day of the equinox

text: True auks (puffins, guillemots and the like) live only in the northern hemisphere. The confusion comes from French, where "pingouin" means auk but was also used for penguins. The goose-sized birds with yellow neck markings in the burrows are clearly penguins, perhaps king penguins.

In the 1860s a French laborer might earn two to four francs a day, so 1,000 francs was something like a year's wages. The price reflects a real collecting mania. The great auk had been hunted to extinction in 1844, and its few surviving eggs fetched fortunes.
quote: a collector would have paid more than 1,000 francs

text: Walruses live only in the Arctic, so finding them at the South Pole is one of Verne's slips. His point about their ivory tusks is accurate, though. They were slaughtered in huge numbers for ivory, hide and oil.

In Greek myth, the shape-shifting "Old Man of the Sea" who herded the seals of the sea-god Poseidon (Neptune). In Homer's Odyssey he naps among his seals on the beach, which is the picture Aronnax has in mind.

Explorers traditionally planted their nation's flag and claimed new land in the name of their sovereign. That's why Aronnax asks "in the name of which sovereign?" Nemo raises his own black flag with a gold N and claims the land for himself, acknowledging no country. Today the Antarctic Treaty of 1959 freezes all national claims to the continent.
quote: I hereby claim this entire part of the globe

text: This is a real folk practice. Storm petrels are so full of oil that islanders in the Faroes and Shetland threaded a wick through a dead bird and burned it as a lamp.
quote: simply fit the bird with a wick

text: Crux, a small, bright, cross-shaped constellation seen from the southern hemisphere. Its long axis points toward the south celestial pole, so sailors used it as the southern stand-in for the North Star, even though no bright star marks the pole itself.
Icebergs melt faster underwater than above, so they become top-heavy and can roll over without warning. Nemo's explanation is sound. Polar sailors gave icebergs a wide berth for exactly this reason.

Augustin Fresnel, a Frenchman, invented the lighthouse lens in 1822: rings of glass prisms that gather a lamp's light into a beam visible more than 20 miles away. Aronnax is comparing the ice walls to that magnifying effect.
quote: biconvex lenses of a world-class lighthouse

text: When the Nautilus ran aground in the Torres Strait earlier in the voyage, Nemo coolly dismissed it as a mere "incident". Aronnax throws the word back at him here, and Nemo's answer, "this time an accident", is the first sign that the danger is real.

In a sealed space, the danger isn't only that oxygen runs out. The carbon dioxide everyone breathes out builds up, and at a few percent it causes pounding headaches, gasping, dizziness and stupor, the exact symptoms Aronnax describes. At higher levels it kills.

Caustic potash, a strong alkali that chemically soaks up carbon dioxide. Aronnax is right. Absorbing CO₂ with alkali chemicals ("scrubbers" of lithium hydroxide or soda lime) is how submarines, spacecraft and divers' rebreathers keep their air breathable. Improvised scrubbers famously saved the Apollo 13 astronauts in 1970.

Electrolysis: passing an electric current through water splits it into hydrogen and oxygen. Aronnax's idea of making breathable air from seawater is sound, and it's how modern nuclear submarines produce their oxygen.
A substance's density compared with water. Ice is about nine-tenths as dense as seawater, so every chunk the diggers cut free floats up and freezes onto the tunnel's ceiling.
quote: an unusual effect of specific gravity

text: Dissolved salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes, which is why roads are salted in winter. Ordinary seawater freezes at about −1.9 °C, so warming the trapped water to −1 °C is just enough to keep it liquid.
quote: salt water freezes only at -2 degrees

text: A still that makes fresh water by boiling seawater and condensing the steam. Steamships began carrying distillers in the mid-19th century. Nemo's inspiration is to turn this ordinary kitchen equipment into a heater for the sea outside.

The archipelago at the tip of South America, today shared by Chile and Argentina. Magellan's crew named it in 1520 for the fires of the local Yaghan and Selk'nam peoples. The winding Strait of Magellan, which separates it from the mainland, was the main alternative to rounding Cape Horn until the Panama Canal opened in 1914.
quote: Tierra del Fuego, the Land of Fire

text: The huge brown seaweeds of these coasts form underwater forests that shelter fish, crabs, seals and sea otters. Giant kelp grows tens of meters long, though not the 300 meters Aronnax claims. "Velp" looks like a slip for "kelp".

Islands in the South Atlantic east of Patagonia, held by Britain since 1833. Their French name, Malouines (after the sailors of Saint-Malo), became the Spanish "Malvinas". Argentina still claims them under that name, and the two countries fought a war over them in 1982.

The Amazon pours out roughly a fifth of all the river water that enters the world's oceans. Its plume of fresh water spreads far out to sea, so Aronnax's claim that it "desalts the sea" for leagues is true.
quote: the mouth of the Amazon River

text: French Guiana, on South America's northeast coast, is still part of France today. In 1868 it was France's notorious penal colony, including Devil's Island, so it would have been an odd sort of refuge. Dutch Guiana, across the Maroni River, is today's Suriname.

Torpedo rays stun their prey with electric organs that can deliver around 200 volts. The weapon called a "torpedo" is named after them. Ancient Greek and Roman doctors used their shocks to numb pain, so Conseil's paralysis is quite realistic.

Manatees and dugongs form the order Sirenia, named after the sirens (mermaids) of myth, and sailors' mermaid sightings are often blamed on them. Aronnax's size and weight are exaggerated. Steller's sea cow, a giant relative up to eight meters long in the Bering Sea, was discovered in 1741 and hunted to extinction within 27 years. It's a grim example of the wipeout Aronnax describes.
quote: manatees, which belong to the order Sirenia

text: Aronnax is repeating the "miasma" theory, the belief that diseases came from bad air rising from rotting matter. Yellow fever is actually a virus spread by mosquitoes, which was proved in Cuba in 1900 by Walter Reed's team, building on the Cuban doctor Carlos Finlay. Alphonse Toussenel was a popular French writer on animals.
quote: this poisoned air causes the yellow fever

text: This strange method is real. Fishermen in the Caribbean, East Africa and northern Australia tied a line to a remora's tail and let it fasten its sucker onto a turtle or big fish, then hauled both in. Columbus's men saw it done off Cuba in 1494.

A sea route through the Arctic islands north of Canada, linking the Atlantic to the Pacific. Explorers hunted for it for three centuries. It was "notorious" above all because of Sir John Franklin's 1845 expedition, which vanished with all 129 men. Nobody had sailed through it by 1868.

It looks like a jellyfish but is a colony of tiny animals working as one. A gas-filled float acts as a sail, and its stinging tentacles can trail for many meters. The sting is agonizing but rarely fatal. The name comes from the float's resemblance to an old sailing warship.

Wealthy ancient Romans paid fortunes for large red mullet. The philosopher Seneca describes diners watching the fish's colors change as it died at the table. The saying means the fish was too valuable for the fisherman to eat himself.
quote: much in demand by rich Romans

text: A sea monster of Scandinavian legend, so huge it could be mistaken for an island. Bishop Erik Pontoppidan's Natural History of Norway (1752) made it famous across Europe. Modern writers suspect that glimpses of giant squid lay behind the legend.

A Swedish churchman (1490–1557) whose great map of Scandinavia, the Carta Marina (1539), and history of the northern peoples teem with sea serpents and ship-crushing monsters. With Pontoppidan, he was the classic source for northern sea-monster lore.

Sailors who survived a disaster often hung a painting of it in a church to thank God or a saint (an "ex-voto"). The French naturalist Denys de Montfort reported one in a chapel at Saint-Malo, the walled port in Brittany, that showed a giant octopus wrapping its arms around a ship.

This really happened. In November 1861 the French warship Alecton, under Lieutenant Frédéric Bouyer, met a giant squid near Tenerife, wounded it and hauled up only a piece of its tail. Bouyer's report to the French Academy of Sciences was greeted with skepticism. Verne's names are slightly altered.

Giant squid (Architeuthis) are real. They reach about 12 meters including tentacles and have the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, three hearts and a parrot-like beak, all as Verne says. They actually have eight arms plus two longer feeding tentacles. Little was known about them in 1868, and one was first photographed alive only in 2004.
The Erinyes of Greek myth, goddesses of vengeance pictured with live snakes for hair.
quote: the serpentine hair of the Furies

text: In Greek myth, the many-headed water serpent killed by Hercules. Every time one head was cut off, two grew back, which is why the endlessly writhing tentacles bring it to mind.

Squid, octopuses and cuttlefish squirt a cloud of dark ink to blind and confuse attackers before escaping, exactly the trick this squid plays. Ink from the cuttlefish (genus Sepia) was used by artists, and "sepia" became the name of a brown color.

Victor Hugo's 1866 novel, set on the Channel island of Guernsey. Its most famous scene is the fisherman Gilliatt's struggle with a monstrous octopus in a sea cave. The book set off an octopus craze in France, so Verne's readers would instantly have connected the two battles.

term: the manuscript and its unsinkable contrivance
text: Essentially a message in a bottle, a time-honored last resort for castaways. Sealed drift bottles were also thrown overboard by 19th-century scientists to trace ocean currents. Aronnax's objection is the obvious one: no one can say where, or whether, it will wash up.

term: Europe's climate and the Gulf Stream
text: Aronnax's warning sounds strikingly modern. Today the Gulf Stream is seen as part of a larger Atlantic circulation (the AMOC) that carries tropical heat north. Climate scientists study whether global warming could weaken it, with exactly the kind of disruption to Europe's weather he imagines.
quote: the climates of Europe would undergo disturbances

text: A headland on North Carolina's Outer Banks where the warm Gulf Stream swings close to shore and meets colder northern water. Its storms and shifting shoals have wrecked so many ships that it's called "the Graveyard of the Atlantic".
quote: across from Cape Hatteras once more

text: A sealed glass tube of chemicals dissolved in alcohol. Sailors believed the crystals forming inside foretold the weather, and Admiral FitzRoy of the Beagle promoted it. In fact the crystals respond mostly to temperature.

On December 23, 1854, the Ansei-Tōkai earthquake struck central Japan. Its tsunami devastated the port of Shimoda (not Tokyo itself) and crossed the Pacific, registering on tide gauges in California hours later. "Tidal wave" is the old name, but these waves are caused by earthquakes, not tides. Verne's speed of about 700 km/h is right for a tsunami in deep water.
To "lie to" (or heave to) is to keep a ship's bow into the waves at minimum speed so it can ride out a storm instead of trying to make progress.
quote: It lay to at half steam

text: Because of the earth's rotation, hurricanes spin counterclockwise in the northern hemisphere and clockwise in the southern. Sailors had learned this "law of storms" in the 1830s and 1840s and used it to steer away from a storm's center.
quote: revolving storms in the southern hemisphere

text: Maury called the Gulf Stream the "Storm King". The contrast between its warm water and the cold air and sea around it breeds violent weather, especially off the American coast. Aronnax overstates things, though: hurricanes are born over warm tropical seas, not by the Gulf Stream alone.

Aronnax's list is real, and it was fresh in readers' memories. The steamer President vanished in 1841, the City of Glasgow in 1854 with about 480 people aboard, and the Pacific in 1856. The Collins liner Arctic sank in 1854 after colliding in fog off Newfoundland, and almost none of the women and children aboard survived. Royal Mail, Inman and Montreal were major steamship companies.
quote: the President, the Pacific, and the City of Glasgow

text: A vast shallow plateau southeast of Newfoundland, where the cold Labrador Current meets the Gulf Stream. The result is thick fog and extraordinarily rich waters. For nearly 500 years it was the world's greatest cod fishery. Aronnax's confidence that the cod's fertility would keep the seas stocked reads painfully now: the stocks collapsed from overfishing, and Canada closed the fishery in 1992.

A telegraph cable on the seabed linking Ireland to Heart's Content in Newfoundland. The first, in 1858, died within weeks. A second snapped during laying (in 1865, not 1863 as Aronnax says). The third succeeded in 1866. News that had taken ten days by ship now crossed in minutes. The American businessman Cyrus Field drove the project through every failure.
quote: where the Atlantic Cable reaches its end point

text: Isambard Kingdom Brunel's giant iron steamship, launched in 1858. At 211 meters it was several times the size of any ship afloat. It failed as a passenger liner but found its true role laying the Atlantic cable. Verne himself crossed the Atlantic aboard it in 1867.

A natural latex from a Malaysian tree that turns hard and waterproof when it sets. It was the only good insulator for undersea cables in the 19th century, which made the Atlantic cable possible. It was also used for early golf balls.

Also called Königgrätz, fought on July 3, 1866, in Bohemia. Prussia crushed Austria in the Seven Weeks' War, clearing the way for a German empire led by Prussia. News of the armistice was among the first reports to cross the new cable.

Cape Clear is on Clear Island off the southwest tip of Ireland. Fastnet Rock, a few miles away, carries a famous lighthouse. It was the last sight of Ireland for emigrant ships bound for America, which earned it the nickname "Ireland's Teardrop".
A ship of the line carrying 74 cannons on two gun decks. It was the standard battleship of the 18th and early 19th centuries, big enough to stand in the line of battle yet fast and handy.

term: Grenada and the Battle of Chesapeake Bay
text: Episodes of France's intervention in the American War of Independence. Admiral d'Estaing captured the British island of Grenada in 1779. On September 5, 1781, the Count de Grasse's fleet drove off a British fleet at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay. That trapped General Cornwallis at Yorktown, and his surrender effectively won American independence.

In 1793 the French Republic replaced the Christian calendar with its own. Years were counted from the founding of the Republic in September 1792, and the months were renamed after the seasons. The "Month of Pasture" is Prairial ("meadow month"), roughly May 20 to June 18. Napoleon abolished the calendar at the end of 1805. Nemo's use of it shows how deeply this anniversary matters to him.

This translation renders the ship's name as "the Avenger". It was the French 74 Vengeur du Peuple ("Avenger of the People"), sunk at the battle the British call the Glorious First of June, 1794. Admiral Howe's fleet fought Villaret de Joyeuse's to stop a convoy carrying American grain to a starving France. The convoy got through. The Revolutionary government spread the story that the crew went down shouting "Long live the Republic!" rather than surrender. In fact the ship had surrendered and British boats rescued several hundred men, but in France the legend became patriotic gospel.

A warship surrendered by lowering ("striking") its flag. Nailing the flag to the mast or deck made striking it impossible, a declaration that the ship would never surrender. It's the origin of the phrase "to nail your colors to the mast".
quote: its flag nailed up on the afterdeck

text: Armored steam warships were brand new in 1868. France's Gloire (1859) was the first ocean-going ironclad. "Double-decker" means two decks of guns. Rams were back in fashion after the Battle of Lissa in 1866, when an Austrian ironclad rammed and sank an Italian one. The Nautilus, with its steel spur, is a ram ship too.
quote: a double-decker ironclad complete with ram

text: A long, narrow pennant at the masthead was flown by commissioned warships, which is how Ned knows this is a naval vessel. A ship's nationality is shown by the flag (ensign) at the gaff, the spar at the top of its fore-and-aft sail. Flying none is a deliberate concealment, as both Aronnax and Nemo notice.
quote: a long pennant streaming from the peak of its mainmast

text: Verne deliberately never names the warship's country. His letters show that he first imagined Nemo as a Polish nobleman avenging Russia's brutal crushing of the Polish uprising of 1863. His publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, wary of offending Russia, persuaded him to keep the nationality secret. Readers have argued about it ever since.
quote: O ship of an accursed nation

text: By long tradition, a black flag meant that no quarter would be given and no prisoners taken. Pirates flew it, and so did rebels fighting to the death. Nemo raises the same flag he planted at the South Pole as his answer to the warship's guns.
quote: Captain Nemo unfurled a black flag

text: Ships at night show a green light on the starboard (right) side, a red one on the port (left) side and a white one on the foremast. Other vessels can then tell which way a ship is heading. Rules like these became standard in the 1860s after a string of collisions.
quote: its green and red running lights

text: On a sailing warship, the drill before battle: stowing or throwing overboard everything that could hamper the guns or fly about as splinters. It survives as an everyday idiom. On the Nautilus it means making the hull perfectly smooth for ramming.

Ironclads wore a thick belt of armor around the waterline, where shells were most dangerous. Below it the hull was far less protected. A blow there lets the sea pour straight in, which is why Nemo submerges a few meters before striking.

term: Spitzbergen, Novaya Zemlya and the Siberian seas
text: Spitzbergen (in today's Svalbard, Norway) and Novaya Zemlya (Russia) are Arctic archipelagos north of Europe. The White Sea, Kara Sea, Gulf of Ob and Lyakhov Islands lie along Russia's Arctic coast. In 1868 they were among the least known waters on earth, so Aronnax's guesses mean the Nautilus has gone almost off the map.
quote: the capes of Spitzbergen or the shores of Novaya Zemlya

text: Edgar Allan Poe's only novel (1838) follows a nightmarish voyage toward the South Pole. It breaks off as a gigantic white "shrouded human figure" rises before the narrator at a polar cataract. Verne admired Poe deeply and wrote an essay on him.

The Moskstraumen, a fierce tidal current with whirlpools off the southern tip of Norway's Lofoten Islands. It's real but was hugely exaggerated in legend. Poe's story "A Descent into the Maelström" (1841), about a fisherman who survives being sucked into it, made it famous, and Verne's account echoes it. Verne places it loosely: the Faroes are far away. The name became the general word for any whirlpool.

A chain of steep islands off northern Norway, well above the Arctic Circle. They were famous for a great winter cod fishery and for the red fishermen's cabins along the shore, so a fisherman's hut is exactly where a castaway would wake up.

Nordkapp, a high cliff on Norway's far northern coast, popularly called the northernmost point of Europe. Coastal steamers linking it with southern Norway were the only practical way home from such remote country.

A book of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally ascribed to King Solomon. The line is from Ecclesiastes 7:24, which the King James Version gives as "That which is far off, and exceeding deep, who can find it out?" "6,000 years ago" follows the old biblical dating of the world. Scholars now date the book to around the 3rd century BC.

The title measures distance traveled, not depth. A league is about 4 kilometers, so 20,000 leagues is roughly 80,000 kilometers, about twice around the earth at the equator. That's the length of the whole journey under the seas.
